title: THEY TRIED TO DESTROY YOU. JESUS SAID TO BLESS THEM.
paragraphs: THEY TRIED TO DESTROY YOU. JESUS SAID TO BLESS THEM.
“Bless Those Who Persecute You” Was Never About Handling a Little Criticism. Paul Was Calling Wounded Believers to Do Something Humanly Impossible.
There is a kind of pain that doesn't leave bruises.
It leaves you staring at the ceiling at 2:17 in the morning, replaying conversations you wish you could forget.
It makes you question people you once trusted. It makes you rehearse arguments in the shower. It makes your stomach tighten when you hear a familiar name.
And sometimes, the person who wounded you is sleeping peacefully while you're still trying to understand how someone could be so cruel.
You didn't start the fight.
You didn't ask to be betrayed.
You weren't looking for enemies.
You were simply trying to live your life, love people, do what was right, and perhaps follow Jesus as faithfully as you knew how.
Then somebody decided to make you suffer for it.
They lied about you.
They twisted your words.
They turned people against you.
They attacked your character, questioned your motives, and made you look like the villain in a story where you were the one bleeding.
And somewhere in the middle of all that pain, you opened your Bible and encountered a sentence that almost felt unbearable.
“Bless them which persecute you: bless, and curse not.” — Romans 12:14 (KJV)
You read it once.
Then again.
And perhaps, for one uncomfortable moment, you wanted to close your Bible.
Because surely Paul couldn't have meant that person.
Surely God understood what they did.
Surely there must be an exception for someone who deliberately humiliated you, betrayed your trust, or made your life miserable.
But here is where the Gospel begins confronting something deeper than the people who hurt us.
What if the person who wounded you never apologizes, but Jesus still refuses to let hatred become the ruler of your heart?
Stay with that question.
Because what Paul wrote in Romans 12 was not advice for surviving an unpleasant comment on social media.
He was describing the supernatural character of people whose lives had been overtaken by the mercy of Jesus Christ.
And once you understand the world behind his words, this command becomes far more disturbing—and far more beautiful—than most of us have ever imagined.
Paul wrote:
εὐλογεῖτε τοὺς διώκοντας ὑμᾶς· εὐλογεῖτε καὶ μὴ καταρᾶσθε.
Eulogeite tous diōkontas hymas; eulogeite kai mē katarasthe.
“Bless them which persecute you: bless, and curse not.” — Romans 12:14 (KJV)
Notice the Greek word διώκοντας (diōkontas).
It comes from the verb diōkō, which can mean to pursue, chase, or persecute. In this context, it describes those who persecute believers.
Paul wasn't merely talking about someone who disagrees with your opinion.
He was speaking about people who actively pursue others with hostility.
People who make faithfulness costly.
People whose opposition can threaten your reputation, livelihood, freedom, relationships, or even your life.
And that matters because the earliest Christians were not living in a world where following Jesus was simply a comfortable religious preference.
They could face rejection, public shame, violence, imprisonment, and death.
Paul himself knew this world intimately.
In Acts 8:3, before his conversion, Saul was entering houses, dragging away men and women, and committing them to prison.
Think about that.
The man who would later command Christians to bless their persecutors had once been one of the persecutors.
He wasn't writing about suffering from a safe distance.
He had caused it.
He had watched the church suffer.
And after encountering the risen Jesus, he would experience persecution himself.
In 2 Corinthians 11:24–25, Paul recounts receiving thirty-nine lashes from Jewish authorities on five occasions, being beaten with rods three times, and being stoned once.
This was not a man who confused persecution with inconvenience.
He knew what human cruelty could do.
He knew what it meant to be opposed.
He knew what it meant to have scars.
Yet he wrote, “Bless, and curse not.”
Why?
Because Paul had encountered a Savior who did not merely teach mercy.
He embodied it.
And that is where this story becomes almost impossible to ignore.
Imagine the road to Damascus.
Saul is traveling with authority to arrest followers of Jesus.
He believes he is defending God.
He is convinced he is righteous.
He is pursuing Christians, not to encourage them, but to bring them into custody.
Then suddenly, everything changes.
A light from heaven.
A voice.
A confrontation that would destroy his old understanding of himself.
“Saul, Saul, why persecutest thou me?” — Acts 9:4 (KJV)
Not merely, “Why are you persecuting My followers?”
Jesus identifies Himself with His suffering people.
Why are you persecuting Me?
The persecutor discovers that the people he has been attacking belong to the risen Lord.
And what does Jesus do?
He confronts Saul, humbles him, and directs him toward the very community he had tried to destroy.
Jesus does not declare Saul innocent.
He does not pretend his actions were harmless.
But neither does He leave Saul beyond the reach of grace.
The man who once hunted Christians becomes a preacher of the Christ he opposed.
The persecutor becomes a witness.
The enemy becomes a brother.
And the church is confronted with an astonishing reality:
The grace of Jesus can reach the very person you would have considered beyond redemption.
That does not mean every persecutor will repent.
It does not mean every enemy will change.
It does not mean every broken relationship will be restored.
But it means no Christian can honestly look at another sinner and declare that the transforming mercy of Christ is powerless to reach them.
Paul knew this better than almost anyone.
Because he was living proof.
Perhaps that is why his command in Romans 12 sounds so uncompromising.
He remembered who he had been.
He remembered what Jesus had done.
And he understood that the Christian life cannot be built upon receiving mercy while refusing to extend it.
But there is something else in the Greek that deserves our attention.
Paul uses the word εὐλογεῖτε (eulogeite)—“bless.”
It is a command.
And he repeats it.
Bless those who persecute you.
Bless, and do not curse.
The repetition gives the instruction unmistakable force.
This is not a passing suggestion.
It is a deliberate call to respond differently from the world around us.
To bless someone is not to announce that their evil was good.
It is not to call betrayal loyalty.
It is not to describe abuse as love.
It is not to pretend injustice never happened.
Rather, in this setting, blessing means refusing to answer hostility with a desire for another person's destruction, and instead seeking what is truly good under God's righteous authority.
That may include praying for their repentance.
Praying that God will expose their sin.
Praying that they will stop harming people.
Praying that truth will prevail.
Praying that the person who has become an instrument of pain might one day become a testimony of redemption.
And sometimes the most honest prayer you can offer is not eloquent at all.
“Lord, I do not know how to bless this person. I am angry. I am hurt. I want them to understand what they did. Please keep my heart from becoming like the evil that wounded me.”
That is not spiritual failure.
That is bringing your struggle into the presence of God instead of disguising it beneath religious language.
Some people have been taught that forgiveness means never admitting they are angry.
So they smile.
They say they're fine.
They quote Scripture.
They keep serving.
But beneath the surface, something is slowly hardening.
And eventually, bitterness begins shaping how they see everyone.
One betrayal becomes a reason to trust nobody.
One cruel person becomes proof that everyone is dangerous.
One painful church experience becomes a reason to withdraw from every Christian community.
One injustice becomes a permanent identity.
And without realizing it, the person who wounded them begins influencing the way they live long after the original injury.
That is one of bitterness's cruelest consequences.
Someone can be absent from your life and still occupy enormous space in your heart.
Jesus does not command us to bless our enemies because He is indifferent to our wounds.
He commands us to love our enemies because He knows what hatred can do to the wounded.
But we must be careful here.
This teaching has sometimes been misused against people who are already suffering.
A woman experiencing domestic violence may be told to forgive and remain silent.
A child harmed by someone in authority may be pressured to protect the offender's reputation.
A church member may be instructed to endure manipulation because “Christians must turn the other cheek.”
That is not a faithful application of Romans 12:14.
Blessing a persecutor does not require remaining within reach of their abuse.
You can pray for someone's repentance and still report their wrongdoing.
You can refuse revenge and still seek justice.
You can forgive someone without restoring access to your life.
You can love an enemy while maintaining firm boundaries.
You can desire someone's salvation while refusing to trust them with responsibilities they have abused.
Romans 12 itself tells believers, “If it be possible, as much as lieth in you, live peaceably with all men” (Romans 12:18, KJV).
Notice those words.
If it be possible.
Paul recognizes that peaceful relationships do not depend on one person alone.
And Romans 13, immediately following this teaching, discusses governing authorities and their responsibility to respond to wrongdoing.
Personal nonretaliation is not the same as abandoning public justice.
God never asks you to rename evil so that someone else can avoid accountability.
Jesus Himself spoke truthfully about sin.
He confronted hypocrisy.
He warned against those who exploited the vulnerable.
And when struck during His questioning, He challenged the injustice of the act (John 18:22–23).
Christlike love is not moral blindness.
It is love governed by truth.
And nowhere is that truth more breathtaking than at the cross.
Picture Calvary.
The sky darkening.
The crowd watching.
The soldiers carrying out the execution.
The religious leaders mocking.
The Son of God hanging between criminals.
The One through whom all things were made is being rejected by the very world He came to save.
And Luke records this extraordinary prayer:
“Father, forgive them; for they know not what they do.” — Luke 23:34 (KJV)

There is a textual detail worth knowing: this sentence is present in many ancient manuscripts of Luke but absent from some other early witnesses. That is why certain modern Bible editions mark it with a footnote.
Even with that textual question, the wider New Testament unmistakably teaches Christ's mercy toward sinners and His call for believers to pray for their persecutors.
Jesus had already taught:
“Love your enemies, bless them that curse you, do good to them that hate you, and pray for them which despitefully use you, and persecute you.” — Matthew 5:44 (KJV)
The cross reveals the depth of that teaching.
Jesus does not deny the evil being committed against Him.
He does not call His executioners innocent.
He does not suggest that sin carries no consequences.
He bears suffering without surrendering to sinful hatred.
And through His death and resurrection, He accomplishes what no wounded human heart could ever accomplish for itself.
Reconciliation with God.
Forgiveness for sinners.
Victory over sin and death.
The hope of a new creation.
This is why Romans 12 cannot be understood properly if we detach it from Romans 1 through 11.
Paul has spent chapter after chapter unfolding the Gospel.
Humanity's sin.
God's righteousness.
Justification by faith.
Peace with God through Jesus Christ.
Life in the Spirit.
The faithfulness and mercy of God.
Then Romans 12 begins:
“I beseech you therefore, brethren, by the mercies of God, that ye present your bodies a living sacrifice, holy, acceptable unto God, which is your reasonable service.” — Romans 12:1 (KJV)
By the mercies of God.
That phrase changes everything.
Paul does not say, “Bless your persecutors so that God will finally love you.”
He does not say, “Forgive perfectly and you will earn salvation.”
He is calling those who have received mercy to live as people transformed by that mercy.
Grace comes first.
Transformation follows.
The Christian does not bless enemies to purchase God's acceptance.
The Christian learns to bless enemies because Christ has already shown undeserved mercy to sinners.
And if we're being painfully honest, that is where the Gospel exposes all of us.
Because we love to imagine ourselves as the innocent person in every biblical story.
We identify with Joseph in the pit.
David pursued by Saul.
Daniel surrounded by enemies.
Stephen facing stones.
But the Gospel requires us to confront another possibility.
Before grace found us, we were not merely wounded people needing comfort.
We were sinners needing reconciliation with God.
Romans 5:8 says:
“But God commendeth his love toward us, in that, while we were yet sinners, Christ died for us.”
And Romans 5:10 goes even further, describing our former condition as enemies reconciled to God through the death of His Son.
Enemies.
That word should silence some of our pride.
We want mercy for our failures and justice for everyone else's.
We want God to understand the reasons behind our worst decisions, while demanding that He judge other people's motives without hesitation.
We remember our own wounds in vivid detail.
But sometimes we forget the wounds our own sins have caused.
Perhaps you have never persecuted a church.
Perhaps you have never dragged anyone into prison.
But have you ever damaged someone's reputation?
Have you ever repeated a story you knew you should have kept private?
Have you ever enjoyed hearing that someone who hurt you was finally suffering?
Have you ever disguised revenge as a prayer request?
Have you ever said, “I forgive them,” while quietly hoping their life would fall apart?
This is not written to crush a wounded person with shame.
It is an invitation to bring the entire heart—its pain and its sin—into the light of Christ.
Because Jesus is not only interested in what happened to you.
He is also interested in what is happening inside you.
And sometimes the hardest enemy to confront is the bitterness we have begun to justify.
Maybe you know exactly what that feels like.
You see their name on Facebook, and your chest tightens.
You hear that something good happened to them, and you feel disappointed.
You hear that something bad happened, and for a split second, you feel satisfied.
Then you realize what your heart has become.
You never wanted to be this person.
You just wanted the pain to stop.
But somewhere along the way, your wound began asking for revenge instead of healing.
And the Lord, in His mercy, is calling you to something different.
Not denial.
Not pretending.
Not instant emotional recovery.
But surrender.
“Lord, I cannot make them repent. I cannot rewrite what they did. I cannot force an apology. But I can place my desire for vengeance into Your hands.”
That is where Romans 12:19 becomes essential.
“Dearly beloved, avenge not yourselves, but rather give place unto wrath: for it is written, Vengeance is mine; I will repay, saith the Lord.”
Paul is drawing from Deuteronomy 32:35, where God declares that vengeance and recompense belong to Him.
The Hebrew word נָקָם (naqam) refers to vengeance or retribution.
In the biblical context, the point is not that wrongdoing is unimportant.
It is that final judgment belongs to the righteous God, not to our wounded impulses.
God sees what people conceal.
He knows what happened behind closed doors.
He knows the words spoken when no one else was listening.
He knows the manipulation, the threats, the lies, and the injustice.
He knows the difference between someone who stumbled and someone who deliberately exploited another person.
And His justice is not weakened by your decision to refuse personal revenge.
You do not have to become cruel to prove that cruelty was wrong.
You do not have to destroy someone to demonstrate that they damaged you.
You do not have to spend the rest of your life prosecuting their case inside your imagination.
You can pursue appropriate justice, tell the truth, protect yourself and others, and still leave ultimate judgment with God.
This is not surrendering truth.
It is surrendering vengeance.
And those are two very different things.
Paul continues:
“Therefore if thine enemy hunger, feed him; if he thirst, give him drink: for in so doing thou shalt heap coals of fire on his head.” — Romans 12:20 (KJV)
Here Paul quotes Proverbs 25:21–22.
The image of burning coals has been interpreted in different ways, including the possibility of provoking shame that leads to repentance or pointing toward divine judgment.
But the surrounding passage makes one thing unmistakable.
Paul is not teaching believers to perform kindness as a secret method of revenge.
He is commanding genuine acts of good rather than retaliation.
And then comes the conclusion:
“Be not overcome of evil, but overcome evil with good.” — Romans 12:21 (KJV)
Read that slowly.
Be not overcome of evil.
There is more than one way for evil to overcome a person.
Sometimes evil overcomes someone through the suffering inflicted upon them.
But sometimes its influence continues when the wounded person begins reproducing the same hatred, dishonesty, or cruelty they once condemned.
The Gospel calls us to resist both.
You may not be able to stop every injustice committed against you.
But by God's grace, you do not have to let that injustice determine the kind of person you become.
This does not happen overnight.
Some wounds require years of healing.
Some situations require counseling, legal protection, wise pastoral care, or sustained support from trustworthy people.
Some relationships cannot safely be restored.
And sometimes obedience begins with nothing more dramatic than refusing to send the angry message you have already typed.
Or choosing not to spread a humiliating story.
Or praying one sentence through tears.
“Jesus, help me want what is right.”
That may seem small.
But small acts of obedience matter.
Not because they make you your own savior.
But because the Savior who redeemed you is patiently transforming you.
Think again about Stephen.
In Acts 7, he is surrounded by people enraged by his testimony.
He is driven outside the city.
Stones begin to fall.
And as he dies, Stephen cries:
“Lord, lay not this sin to their charge.” — Acts 7:60 (KJV)
This was not a man responding to a rude remark.
He was being killed.
And among those connected with that scene was a young man named Saul, who consented to Stephen's death, as Acts 8:1 records.
Scripture does not say Stephen's prayer directly caused Saul's conversion.
We must not invent that connection.
But the sequence is still staggering.
A Christian dies praying for mercy.
A persecutor approves of his death.
And later, that persecutor meets the risen Christ and becomes an apostle.
The story does not promise that every enemy you pray for will become another Paul.
But it reminds us that God's grace can write chapters no human being could have predicted.
And perhaps that is the truth someone reading this desperately needs.
The person who betrayed you may never apologize.
The people who believed the lies may never publicly correct them.
The opportunity you lost may never return.
The relationship may never be what it once was.
You may never receive the earthly closure you wanted.
But your future is not chained to their repentance.
Your obedience is not dependent on their apology.
And your identity in Christ is not determined by their accusations.
They may have written a painful chapter in your life.
But they do not hold the pen that writes your eternity.
Jesus Christ does.
And His Gospel does not merely offer you a better reputation.
It offers you a new life.
A life where the sinner can repent.
Where the ashamed can find forgiveness.
Where the wounded can receive comfort.
Where the bitter can learn mercy.
Where the persecutor can become a brother.
Where the betrayed can be restored without pretending betrayal was harmless.
Where justice and grace are not enemies.
Where the cross tells the truth about sin while revealing the immeasurable mercy of God.
This is what we mean when we say:
Not that every scandal disappears.
Not that every consequence is erased.
Not that the past becomes imaginary.
But that Jesus Christ can redeem sinners, restore what sin has devastated according to His wisdom, and give His people a future no longer ruled by condemnation and despair.
Perhaps right now, one name is sitting heavily on your heart.
You have been thinking about that person since the beginning of this article.
You know what they said.
You remember what they did.
You still feel the cost.
I am not asking you to pretend it was acceptable.
I am not asking you to contact them.
I am not asking you to return to an unsafe situation.
I am asking you to consider whether the Lord is inviting you to place something into His hands that you have been carrying alone.
Maybe it is the desire to retaliate.
Maybe it is the need for everyone to hear your side.
Maybe it is the belief that you cannot move forward until someone finally admits the truth.
Maybe it is the fear that forgiving them would mean what happened did not matter.
But forgiveness does not erase truth.
And blessing does not cancel accountability.
You can entrust someone to God's justice while refusing to become the instrument of personal revenge.
You can pray for their repentance without giving them another opportunity to hurt you.
You can acknowledge the depth of your pain while trusting Christ to begin healing what you cannot repair.
And if you are not ready to pray for them today, begin by telling Jesus the truth about that too.
He already knows.
There is no need to perform strength in front of the One who sees your weakness.
You can say:

“Lord Jesus, You know what happened. You know what I lost. You know how angry I still am. Forgive me for the ways bitterness has taken root in my heart. Give me wisdom to seek truth and justice without revenge. Protect me from further harm. Teach me to pray for repentance where there is sin, healing where there is pain, and mercy where I have become hard. I cannot change another person's heart, but I surrender my own to You. Thank You for dying for sinners and rising again. Help me live as someone who has received Your grace. Amen.”
And maybe, for the first time in a long time, you do not need to have the final word.
You can let God be God.
Or perhaps your prayer is, “Lord, help me forgive without compromising truth.”

You do not have to expose private details or name the person who hurt you. Sometimes a few honest words can become the beginning of a meaningful conversation with other believers who understand the struggle.
Someone who feels trapped in anger may need to hear that healing is possible.
There may also be someone on your Facebook friends list who is silently fighting this battle.
Someone who has been betrayed.
Someone who has stopped trusting people.
Someone who believes their anger is the only thing protecting them from being hurt again.
Not simply to increase its reach, but because a biblical reminder offered at the right moment may help someone turn toward Christ instead of surrendering to despair.
We are not building a community around perfect people.
We are gathering people who know they need a perfect Savior.
And for those who want to help carry this Gospel-centered mission further, I want to invite you into something more personal.
If you have been blessed through Gospel Warrior and desire to glorify God by helping others receive biblical truth, this is one meaningful opportunity to participate.
God's grace is not for sale. Your salvation cannot be purchased. And no monthly payment can replace genuine repentance, faith, obedience, or love.
As 2 Corinthians 9:7 teaches, giving should not be done grudgingly or under compulsion, because God loves a cheerful giver.
Our hope is that these resources will help people open their Bibles, examine their lives, grow in sound doctrine, persevere through suffering, and become more faithful disciples of Jesus.
But above everything else, remember why this ministry exists.
Not to make Gospel Warrior famous.
Not to make any writer indispensable.
Not to turn suffering into entertainment or faith into a transaction.
We want people to see Jesus.
The Jesus who confronted Saul on the Damascus road.
The Jesus who forgives sinners without excusing sin.
The Jesus who teaches His followers to love their enemies.
The Jesus who endured the cross and rose victorious from the grave.
The Jesus who still calls wounded, angry, exhausted, imperfect people to repentance, faith, and a new way of life.
What if the person who hurt you never apologizes?
What if they never acknowledge what happened?
What if they continue telling their version of the story?
Will you allow their actions to determine the condition of your soul?
Or will you bring your pain to the Savior who knows what it means to suffer unjustly?
You do not need to deny the wound.
You do not need to rush the healing.
You do not need to call evil good.
But you can begin to release the desire for vengeance into the hands of the One who judges righteously.
Because the greatest miracle in this story may not be that your enemy changes.
It may be that, through the grace of Jesus Christ, you refuse to become the person your suffering was tempting you to be.
And one day, when you remember what they did, perhaps the pain will no longer be the loudest voice in the room.
Perhaps the mercy of Christ will be.
They may never ask you for forgiveness—but through Jesus, their cruelty does not have to become the final chapter of your heart.
